title: Logic Pro 12 Update
intro: Logic Pro 12 arrived in January 2026 and it is an Apple silicon release — Intel Macs stop here. The headline additions are the Synth Player and Chord ID, which together change how a track gets arranged. This section covers what is new, plus the upgrade playbook for surviving any major release.

notice.title: One requirement before anything else
notice.text: Logic Pro 12 requires an Apple silicon Mac running macOS 15.6 or later. There is no Intel version. If you are still on an Intel machine, Logic Pro 11 is the end of the road — plan around that before you update anything.

tips.t: Synth Player is the third Session Player
tips.d: Create a Session Player track and choose Synth. It generates synth parts that follow your Chord track the same way Bass Player and Keyboard Player do — so a progression can arrange itself across three instruments.

tips.t: Pick the Synth Keyboard style before you touch anything else
tips.d: Simple Pad for a sustained harmonic bed, Modulated Pad when you want movement, Rhythmic Chords when the part needs to drive. Same chords, three completely different jobs.

tips.t: Synth Bass ships with three distinct characters
tips.d: 808 Bass for trap-leaning low end, Pump Bass for filtered movement, Sequenced Bass for driving sixteenths. Audition all three before you start editing the pattern.

tips.t: Intensity changes tone, not just level
tips.d: On Pump Bass especially, raising Intensity opens the filter as well as pushing the level. It is the fastest way to make a bassline build without drawing a single automation point.

tips.t: Point Synth Player at a third-party synth
tips.d: The performance engine and the sound source are separate. Synth Player can drive any Audio Unit, and external hardware too, so you keep the chord-following performance and choose your own sound.

tips.t: Chord ID reads chords off audio, not just MIDI
tips.d: Drag in a guitar demo, a piano take or a rough bounce and Chord ID analyses it and writes the progression to the Chord track in seconds. It is the fastest route from an idea to a working arrangement.

tips.t: Chord ID gets the harmonic rhythm, not just the chords
tips.d: It works out when the chords change as well as what they are, so the Chord track lands on the right bars instead of needing to be dragged into place afterwards.

tips.t: Everything downstream follows the Chord track
tips.d: Once Chord ID has populated it, Session Players, the Step Sequencer and arpeggiators all follow the progression. One analysis pass can arrange three parts at once.

tips.t: Run Chord ID on your own old bounces
tips.d: The fastest way to rebuild a session you have lost is to drag the bounce in, let Chord ID read the changes, and start again from a chord track you know is correct.

tips.t: Preview sound packs before you download them
tips.d: The rebuilt Sound Library plays an audio preview of any pack before you install it, and lets you delete packs you never use to get the disk space back.

tips.t: Re-run Mastering Assistant on older masters
tips.d: Genre detection and the interface both changed in 12. A master you processed under Logic 11 is worth analysing again before you call it finished.

tips.t: Logic Pro 12 drops Intel Macs entirely
tips.d: It requires an Apple silicon Mac and macOS 15.6 or later. If you are on Intel, Logic Pro 11 is the last version you can run — check your machine before you plan an upgrade.

tips.t: Never update in the middle of a paid project
tips.d: The one rule that matters. Finish and deliver, then update. A new version halfway through a mix is a self‑inflicted deadline problem.

tips.t: Keep the previous version installed alongside the new one
tips.d: Before updating, duplicate Logic Pro in your Applications folder and rename the copy with its version number. macOS will run both, and you have an instant fallback.

tips.t: Back up your key commands, templates and channel strip settings
tips.d: These live in your user Library, not in the app. Export key commands from the Key Commands window and copy your templates folder somewhere safe.

tips.t: Consolidate and archive your three most important projects
tips.d: Project > Consolidate on each, then copy them to a separate drive. If the new version changes something, you have untouched originals.

tips.t: Check your critical third‑party plugins against the new version first
tips.d: Plugin developers lag major DAW releases. Check their compatibility pages before you update, not after.

tips.t: Note your current I/O and buffer settings
tips.d: Major updates sometimes reset audio device preferences. A screenshot of your Audio settings takes five seconds and saves a confusing afternoon.

tips.t: Update macOS and Logic separately, a week apart
tips.d: If something breaks, you want to know which of the two did it.

tips.t: Open an old project and audit every insert
tips.d: Look for greyed‑out or missing plugins on every channel. Do this before you assume everything migrated cleanly.

tips.t: Rebuild your templates rather than opening old ones
tips.d: New versions add track types, settings and defaults that an old template will not have. Rebuilding takes an hour and you get every new default for free.

tips.t: Re‑check Settings > Advanced and turn everything on again
tips.d: Advanced Tools sometimes resets. If half the program has disappeared, this is the first place to look.

tips.t: Read the new Key Commands list for additions
tips.d: Open ⌥K and sort by command name. New features arrive with new commands, many of them unassigned by default.

tips.t: Run the Sound Library update fully before working
tips.d: Logic Pro > Sound Library > Download All Available Sounds. A half‑downloaded library produces silent tracks that look fine.

tips.t: Test your bounce path end to end before you need it
tips.d: Bounce a short section to every format you deliver in. Export bugs are the ones that bite at the worst possible moment.

tips.t: Give yourself a deliberate hour to explore
tips.d: Not on a project. Open a scratch session and use every new feature once. An hour of play beats a month of accidental discovery.
